title: What Expansion Actually Means
author: Kathleen Schafer
source: Extraordinarily Ordinary: A Field Guide for Being Human (Substack)
summary: Kathleen Schafer's essay recasts expansion — in both the personal and leadership sense — not as acquiring more or becoming someone different, but as becoming more fully and honestly who one already is. The piece is framed around the threshold of May as a seasonal metaphor for the moment when emergence (private formation, taking root) shifts into expression (public growth, visible contribution). At the heart of the article is a question Schafer identifies as one of the most important in leadership: 'How do I build the better new while I'm still standing inside the old?' Her answer is conscious choice — holding two realities simultaneously: the truth of what currently exists (with its limitations and seductions) and the vision of what could be, without letting the existing system define the outer boundary of imagination. She argues that this dual-awareness capacity is the distinguishing feature of leaders who transform systems versus those who, despite sincere intentions, eventually become shaped by the broken structures they entered to change. True expansion, in her framework, requires rooting into personal truth — values, purpose, and non-negotiables — as the precondition for sustainable growth. The old model of leadership, she argues, optimized for striving, proving, and exhausting oneself in the name of growth; authentic leadership expansion is something different: becoming more honest, more aligned, more joyfully present to the work one is actually here to do. The piece ends with a seedling image: it does not argue with the darkness it moved through, does not mistake resistance for impossibility, and trusts its nature as it reaches toward the sun while staying rooted in the earth.
points: The most common leadership failure mode Schafer identifies is entering broken systems with sincere transformation intent and, without noticing the gradual drift, being shaped by them rather than shaping them — losing the thread back to one's own original intention until one becomes part of what one set out to change.

The crucial distinction between striving and expanding: the old model of leadership optimized for proving, scaling, and exhausting oneself, whereas true expansion is about becoming more fully who you already are — more honest, more aligned, more genuinely present to the specific work that is yours to do.

Conscious choice is the only workable answer to Schafer's core leadership question: leaders must maintain dual awareness of the truth of what exists and the vision of what could be, refusing to let the system's current limits define the horizon of what is imaginable.

Values, purpose, and non-negotiables — not external validation or institutional alignment — are the ground from which sustainable leadership growth must proceed; without that internal truth as a reference point, even well-intentioned leaders cannot hold their orientation in environments that reward speed, conformity, and quiet compliance.

The soul expands when the life can hold more honesty: alignment between inner truth and outward action is not merely a virtue ideal but the structural precondition for integrity — what grows from alignment has integrity; what grows from performance does not.
quotes: If we want to create the shifts we long to see, we must place ourselves more fully into life. Not as performance. Not by becoming louder or faster or more polished. By becoming more honest. More aligned. More genuinely available to the work that is ours to do.

How do I build the better new while I'm still standing inside the old? I've held that question for a long time. The truest answer I know is conscious choice. We move toward what we are creating by staying awake to what is, its limitations, its pull, its seductions, while keeping ourselves oriented toward something larger.

Without that grounding, even the most well-meaning leaders lose their way. They step into broken structures sincerely hoping to transform them, and slowly, without quite noticing, they begin to be shaped by them. They lose the thread back to their own intention. They become, in some cases, part of the very thing they set out to change.

Not the truth of the system. The truth of who we are inside it. What we value. What we came to offer. What we will not surrender even in environments that reward speed, conformity, or quiet compliance.

The old model taught us to strive. To prove and scale and exhaust ourselves in the name of growth. But true expansion is something else altogether. It is not about becoming someone different. It is about becoming more fully, more honestly, more joyfully who we already are.
The soul expands when the life can hold more honesty. What grows from alignment has integrity.

The seedling does not argue with the darkness it has moved through. It doesn't mistake resistance for impossibility. It trusts its nature. It stays rooted as it grows. It reaches toward the sun without severing itself from the earth. That is leadership in this moment.
